displayQuote: Hope in reality is the worst of all evils, because it prolongs the torments of man

meta.title: Who really said "Hope in reality is the worst of all evils"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Nietzsche — Human, All Too Human (1878), aphorism 71, titled 'Die Hoffnung'. The circulating English is Helen Zimmern's public-domain translation, and it is not, as often claimed, a line from the novel When Nietzsche Wept.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hope in reality is the worst of all evils'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Nietzsche: Human, All Too Human I §71, 'Die Hoffnung' — his reading of Pandora's jar. The popular English is Zimmern's 1909 translation, free to reuse.

answer.label: Verified — Human, All Too Human, 1878
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and locatable to the aphorism: Menschliches, Allzumenschliches (Human, All Too Human), Volume I, 1878, aphorism 71 — which Nietzsche titled ‘Die Hoffnung’ (‘Hope’). The German closes: ‘sie ist in Wahrheit das übelste der Übel, weil sie die Qual der Menschen verlängert.’ The English everyone quotes is Helen Zimmern’s translation, lightly re-cut — and it is public domain.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Zeus wollte nämlich, daß der Mensch, auch noch so sehr durch die anderen Übel gequält, doch das Leben nicht wegwerfe, sondern fortfahre, sich immer von neuem quälen zu lassen. Dazu gibt er dem Menschen die Hoffnung: sie ist in Wahrheit das übelste der Übel, weil sie die Qual der Menschen verlängert.
trail: We checked the German directly. The aphorism is titled ‘Die Hoffnung,’ it is about hope, and the word in the closing clause is die Hoffnung. A claim circulates that Nietzsche really wrote this of pity (Mitleid) and that the quote is therefore altered — that claim is false; the German does not support it.

The circulating English is Helen Zimmern’s: ‘Therefore he gives man hope,—in reality it is the worst of all evils, because it prolongs the torments of man.’ The popular form just re-cuts her clause to start with ‘Hope’ Zimmern text ↗.

The other early English, Alexander Harvey’s of 1908, reads ‘the greatest of evils for it lengthens the ordeal of man’ — which is not the circulating wording. That isolates Zimmern as the source of the version you have read Harvey 1908 ↗.
source.excerptNote: Nietzsche’s German. The passage is his reading of Pandora’s jar: hope is not the consolation left behind after the evils escaped — it is the evil that stayed, and Zeus left it there deliberately.

source.rightsNote: Free to reuse, in both languages. Nietzsche died in 1900, so the German is public domain worldwide; Helen Zimmern’s English was published in 1909/1910 and she died in 1934, so her translation is public domain in the United States and in life-plus-seventy countries alike. Alexander Harvey’s 1908 version is a safe alternative. Do not quote the modern translations — Hollingdale (1986) and Faber–Lehmann (1995) are under copyright, and neither produces this wording anyway. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) wrote in aphorisms, which makes him the most quotable of philosophers and the most misquoted — a stray sentence of his survives detachment from its argument better than almost anyone’s. Human, All Too Human (1878) marks his break with Wagner and with Schopenhauer’s pessimism, and is the book where he began dismantling comforting ideas one short entry at a time. Hope got entry 71.

misattribution.heading: Two things people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right and the source is exact. What circulates instead are two confident corrections that are themselves mistaken — which is why this page exists.

items.why: A widely repeated claim holds that the aphorism is about Mitleid (pity) and that ‘hope’ is a corruption. We checked the German: the aphorism is titled ‘Die Hoffnung,’ and the closing clause reads sie ist in Wahrheit das übelste der Übel — sie being hope. The quote is about hope.

Irvin Yalom’s 1992 novel When Nietzsche Wept gives its Nietzsche character a compressed version, and because far more people have read the novel than aphorism 71, many assume the line was invented for it. Yalom was paraphrasing the real text.

items.who: Helen Zimmern, not the modern ones
items.why: The wording you know is Zimmern’s, which matters practically: hers is public domain, while the Hollingdale and Faber–Lehmann translations are in copyright — and neither of those produces this phrasing.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Nietzsche, Human, All Too Human I §71 (1878), in an aphorism he titled ‘Hope’ — and the familiar English is Helen Zimmern’s public-domain translation read it ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is a deliberate inversion of the story everyone knows. In the usual telling of Pandora’s jar, all the evils fly out and hope remains behind as mankind’s consolation. Nietzsche reads the same myth and concludes that hope stayed in the jar because it was the worst thing in it.

The cruelty is in the mechanism, not the mood: Zeus wants humans to keep suffering rather than throw life away, so he supplies the one thing that makes suffering bearable enough to continue. Hope is not a comfort in this reading — it is the reason the torment can be extended.
detailsBody: Zimmern, 1909: ‘in reality it is the worst of all evils, because it prolongs the torments of man’ — the ancestor of the popular wording.
Harvey, 1908: ‘the greatest of evils for it lengthens the ordeal of man’ — same German, different English, never went viral.
Both are public domain; both are faithful. The difference is entirely a translator’s ear.
Nietzsche’s own word is übelste — the most evil, the worst — playing against Übel, the evils that escaped the jar. English cannot easily keep that echo.
context.pull: Hope stayed in the jar not as the consolation, but as the worst thing in it.
